title: Choosing hiring models: employment, geography and delivery
objectives: Describe the three dimensions of the page's comparison (employment type, geography, delivery model) and see why its matrix mixes them
Compute time-zone overlap for a location pair and judge whether a work pattern is feasible
Build a cost per effective engineer-year model that includes recruiting, ramp, management overhead and asynchronous loss
Show how sensitive the ranking of options is to the page's unsourced savings percentages
Recommend a hybrid with a decision rule, risks and a review point, and say what legal and tax questions go to advisers

sources.title: Engineering Hiring Models Comparison
sources.reviewDepth: Page content retrieved as an automated summary; re-read the page itself before relying on any figure.

verificationNotes: NOT LEGAL OR TAX ADVICE. Worker classification, employer of record arrangements, IP assignment, data protection, severance and cross-border payroll differ by country and are matters for qualified advisers. The page mentions IR35 (a UK tax classification regime) only in passing; this lesson does not explain it.

The page compares options on three dimensions (permanent versus contractor; onshore, nearshore and offshore; embedded, software factory and burst capacity) and gives a six-row matrix rating speed to ramp, cost arbitrage, control, IP and context retention, and management overhead. Its figures are unsourced: nearshore savings of 20% to 40%, offshore savings of 50% to 70% (50% to 60% for a factory), overlap of 4 to 8 hours for nearshore and 1 to 3 for offshore, onshore permanent ramp of 2 to 4 months, contractor availability of 1 to 2 weeks and nearshore embedded of 2 to 4 weeks. It cites only a general Wikipedia article on IT outsourcing.

The retrieved summary flagged these points: 'EOR' (employer of record) appears in the matrix but is never explained; the 'Operating Models Overview' heading has no content; onshore is said to have 'zero legal and regulatory complexity' though the page itself notes classification risk for contractors that can apply domestically; contractors are said to offer 'immediate availability' while the matrix says 1 to 2 weeks; the matrix mixes location, employment type and delivery model, so combinations such as onshore or offshore embedded are missing and categories overlap; offshore savings differ between text (50% to 70%) and matrix (50% to 60% for a factory) without explanation; the 'fixed cost' label for factories, 'direct control over quality' for embedded models and the claim that high-performing organisations 'typically' use hybrids are unsupported; and no decision framework is given despite the stated goal.

The page does not cover total cost of ownership, recruiting fees or currency effects, legal detail on data protection, IP ownership or contracts, vendor selection or SLA design, how to measure vendor quality, transition from outsourced to in-house work, retention or attrition data, case studies or team-size thresholds.

The cost model, sensitivity analysis and break-even calculation in this lesson are Original Academy material run in Python. Every input (salary, on-costs, recruiting fee, rates, ramp, savings, management overhead, productivity loss and vendor margin) is an invented ASSUMPTION. The model leaves out quality and rework cost, attrition, severance, exchange-rate movement and cultural fit, so its output ranks illustrative scenarios and is not a recommendation for any real choice. Time-zone overlap uses standard UTC offsets without daylight saving.

sections.heading: The page's comparison
sections.body:
The page argues that no single hiring model fits every need and that leaders should choose by company stage, technical complexity, budget and strategic focus. It compares options along three dimensions.

Employment type. Permanent employees hold core IP, architecture and culture (strengths: alignment, institutional memory, commitment; weaknesses: high fixed cost, slow recruiting, severance liability, notice periods). Contractors and freelancers fill gaps or short milestones (fast, flexible, operating expense; higher hourly rates, classification risk, weak alignment, context lost at the end).

Geography. Onshore (headquarters country): same time zone and culture, premium cost, small talent pool. Nearshore (adjacent time zones): the page cites 4 to 8 hours of overlap and 20% to 40% savings. Offshore (distant time zones): 50% to 70% savings, 1 to 3 hours of overlap, communication latency and quality variance.

Delivery model. Embedded staff augmentation puts external engineers inside internal teams under internal managers. A software factory hands a scope to a vendor under deliverables and SLAs. Burst capacity brings in temporary high-throughput resources for a window, for example 3 to 6 months.

Strategic guidance: protect the core and flex the perimeter, watch the asynchronous tax, and avoid the vendor trap by requiring technical standards, automated tests and client ownership of repositories and pipelines. Its conclusion is that most high-performing organisations use a hybrid.

sections.heading: Reading the matrix critically
sections.body:
The matrix gives six rows. Notice what each row actually is: 'Onshore Perm' is an employment type in a location; 'Nearshore Embedded' is a location and a delivery model; 'Offshore Factory' is a location and a delivery model; 'Burst Capacity' is a delivery model with no location. Because the rows mix dimensions, you cannot read across them as like-for-like, and several real options are missing, such as an offshore embedded contractor or an onshore software factory. Build your own comparison with the dimensions separated: who employs the person (you, a contractor, a vendor, an employer of record), where they sit, and how their work is managed (embedded in your team, delivered against a scope, or temporary).

Treat the numbers as hypotheses. The savings percentages, overlap hours and ramp times are unsourced, vary by country, seniority and year, and ignore the fees that intermediaries charge. 'Employer of record' is a service that legally employs someone on your behalf in their country; it adds a fee, and the page never explains it. 'Zero legal complexity' onshore is plainly too strong: contractor classification, employment law and data protection apply at home too.

Also notice what the page leaves out that decides real cases: quality and rework, attrition, how much of the work needs deep product context, security and data constraints on who may access what, and the cost of managing the arrangement. Those are in the model below.

sections.heading: Time zones are arithmetic
sections.body:
Overlap hours are easy to compute and often skipped. With both sides working 09:00 to 17:00 local time, the overlap is the intersection of the two intervals in a common time.

Examples (standard offsets, no daylight saving, for illustration): UTC and India (UTC+5:30) overlap 2.5 hours, consistent with the page's offshore 1 to 3; UTC and South Africa (UTC+2) overlap 6 hours; US east coast (UTC-5) and UTC overlap 3 hours; US east coast and Brazil (UTC-3) overlap 6; UTC and the Philippines (UTC+8) overlap none. So the page's 'nearshore 4 to 8 hours' does not hold for every pair that is geographically near, and a pair that sounds distant can have usable overlap if the workday shifts.

Use the overlap to decide the work pattern. With 2.5 hours, synchronous pairing and meetings must fit into that window, so design the work for asynchronous handoffs: clear interfaces, written decisions, domain-bounded tasks (the page's advice). With 6 hours, daily collaboration is realistic. Decide whether either side will shift hours, and who bears the inconvenience.

sections.heading: A cost per effective engineer-year
sections.body:
Salary or rate alone misleads. Compare the cost per effective engineer-year: total cost over a horizon divided by the productive years delivered. Include recruiting fees, ramp-up at reduced productivity, management overhead, and a productivity loss for coordination across time zones. The formula used here: cost per effective engineer-year = (annual loaded cost x (1 + management overhead) + (recruiting fee + ramp loss) / years) / (1 - productivity loss), where ramp loss is the annual loaded cost x ramp years x 0.5.

All inputs are invented ASSUMPTIONS. An onshore engineer has a salary of 120,000 with 25% on-costs, a loaded cost of 150,000. Recruiting costs 20% of salary (24,000), and ramp-up is three months at half productivity.
- Onshore permanent: annual 150,000; recruiting and ramp add 42,750. Over 1 year the cost per effective year is about 192,750; over 3 years about 164,250.
- Onshore contractor: 95 an hour for 1,700 hours is 161,500 a year, a 5% management overhead, two weeks of ramp and no recruiting fee. Over 1 year about 172,700; over 3 years about 170,600.
- Nearshore embedded: a 30% saving on the onshore loaded cost (105,000), 10% management overhead, 5% productivity loss, one month of ramp. About 126,200 over 1 year and 123,100 over 3.
- Offshore: a 60% saving (60,000), 15% management overhead, a 25% productivity loss for the asynchronous tax, three months of ramp. About 102,000 over 1 year and 95,300 over 3.

Break-even: because the permanent route carries 42,750 of upfront recruiting and ramp cost, and the contractor costs about 1,631 a month more (169,575 a year against 150,000), the contractor is cheaper for the first 24 months or so of continuous use in this model, a result few expect and one that depends entirely on the inputs. If you need the person for under about two years and the work does not need deep institutional context, the contractor's higher rate is not obviously the more expensive option; the page's 'high fixed cost' for permanent staff is real, but so is the contractor premium.

Now stress the savings assumption, since the page's percentages are unsourced. If the offshore saving is only 50%, management overhead 20% and the asynchronous loss 35%, the 3-year cost is about 143,300, close to the onshore permanent figure of 164,250. If the vendor or an employer of record adds a 25% margin to the 60% saving case, the 3-year figure rises from 95,300 to about 119,200. The ranking of options changes with plausible inputs, which is why the model should use your quotes and your measured productivity loss, not the page's ranges.

What the model leaves out matters as much: rework when quality varies, the cost of attrition and knowledge loss when a contract ends, security and data constraints, and the effect on the team's culture, such as the page's 'first-class and second-class' developer dynamics for embedded staff. Use the model to see which assumptions drive the answer, then investigate those.

sections.heading: A decision rule and the hybrid
sections.body:
The page states 'protect the core, flex the perimeter' and says most high-performing organisations use a hybrid, without evidence. Turn it into a rule you can apply.

Classify each piece of work on three questions. How much deep, lasting product and architecture context does it need? How well can it be specified as an interface or scope? How sensitive is the data or the security exposure? High context, poor specification and high sensitivity point to permanent in-house staff. Well-specified, low-context work with clear acceptance tests suits a vendor or factory, with the page's guardrails: your standards, automated tests, your repositories and pipelines. Short-term spikes suit burst capacity, but plan the onboarding cost and hold the quality gates, or you inherit technical debt.

Then decide where to cap exposure: no more than a stated share of critical-path components owned only by external staff; knowledge transfer built into every contract; exit costs priced in advance. Write the decision as an ADR with the trigger for review, for example 'review in six months or when the external share of critical components exceeds a third'.

Tax and legal questions go to advisers before you sign: classification of contractors, whether an employer of record is needed, IP assignment, data protection and cross-border payroll. This lesson does not answer them.

workedExample.title: Adding eight engineers for a 12-month platform migration (invented numbers, not Cretek data)
workedExample.body:
Cretek needs eight more engineers for a 12-month migration, with a likely need for four of them afterwards. Headquarters is on UTC+2 (South Africa) in this example.

Step 1, split the work. Three kinds of work: (a) the migration architecture and the data model (high context, high sensitivity); (b) well-specified service rewrites against existing tests (low context, clear interface); (c) a six-week data clean-up before cut-over (burst).

Step 2, map to models. (a) permanent, hired in-house: 2 engineers. (b) an embedded nearshore contractor team of 4 in a time zone with 6 hours of overlap, under Cretek managers, with Cretek owning the repositories and pipeline. (c) burst contractors for six weeks, 2 engineers.

Step 3, cost per effective year. Using the lesson's illustrative model: permanent about 192,750 per effective year over one year (164,250 over three), nearshore about 126,200 over one year. Burst contractors: two engineers at the contractor rate for 6 weeks, about 95 an hour for 240 hours each, which is 45,600 for two before any ramp or management cost. Because six weeks is short, the two-week ramp is a large share of the period and should be priced in, not ignored.

Step 4, check the overlap. The nearshore team has 6 hours of overlap, so pairing and design discussions fit in the shared window; the migration architecture decisions stay with the two permanent engineers, written as ADRs the team can read. If the nearshore team were in a distant zone with 2.5 hours of overlap, the same plan would need clearer interfaces and a longer review cycle, and the model's 25% asynchronous loss would apply instead of 5%.

Step 5, sensitivity. If nearshore savings are 20% not 30%, and management overhead is 15%, the cost per effective year rises to about 150,500 for one year (computed with the lesson's model); the decision still favours the nearshore team over onshore permanent staff for this part, but the gap is smaller, so the team asks the vendor for a quote and an exit schedule before committing.

Step 6, guardrails and exits. Cretek owns the repositories and CI/CD, requires automated test coverage on rewritten services (the page's guardrail), requires written knowledge transfer as a deliverable, and prices an exit: a three-month handover at a stated rate. The external share of critical-path components is capped at one third.

Step 7, questions for advisers. Contractor classification in the contractor's country and in South Africa, whether an employer of record is needed, IP assignment, data protection for the customer data the migration touches, and any cross-border payroll rules. Marked 'requires verification with counsel and tax advisers'.

Step 8, review. At six months: delivery against the plan, rework rate on rewritten services, knowledge held only by externals, and the survey of engineers on how well the blended team works.

What is unverified: all rates, savings and the model are invented, and the burst-contractor figure in step 3 excludes ramp and management cost.

misconceptions: Comparing hourly rates instead of cost per effective engineer-year.
Treating the page's savings percentages and overlap hours as established facts.
Believing onshore has no legal complexity.
Assuming nearshore always means usable overlap. Compute it.
Assuming a contractor is always the expensive option. It depends on duration and fees.
Outsourcing work that needs deep, lasting context and then losing the knowledge when the contract ends.
Signing an outsourcing agreement without owning the repositories and pipeline.
learn.explainTask: In 150 words or fewer, explain to a CFO why the cheapest hourly rate is not the cheapest way to add engineering capacity.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the overlap in 09:00 to 17:00 local working hours between UTC and India (UTC+5:30)?
knowledgeCheck.why: India's 09:00 to 17:00 is 03:30 to 11:30 UTC, so the overlap with 09:00 to 17:00 UTC is 09:00 to 11:30: 2.5 hours.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why is the page's matrix hard to read across?
options: Its rows mix employment type, location and delivery model, so categories overlap and combinations are missing
knowledgeCheck.why: The retrieved summary noted that the matrix combines location, employment type and delivery model, so it is not a like-for-like comparison.

knowledgeCheck.question: In the lesson's model, the permanent route has 42,750 of upfront recruiting and ramp cost and costs about 1,631 a month less than the contractor. Roughly how long until the permanent route is cheaper?
knowledgeCheck.why: (42,750 - about 3,100 contractor ramp) / 1,631 is about 24 months. The result depends entirely on the assumed inputs.

knowledgeCheck.question: What happens to the offshore 3-year cost per effective year when the saving falls to 50%, overhead rises to 20% and asynchronous loss to 35%?
options: It rises to about 143,300, near the onshore permanent figure
knowledgeCheck.why: Plausible changes to the page's unsourced assumptions close most of the gap, so the ranking is sensitive to them.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which is a fair statement about 'employer of record' on the page?
options: It appears in the matrix but is never explained; it is a service that legally employs someone on your behalf and adds a fee
It is a type of contractor tax
It is the same as offshore
knowledgeCheck.why: The retrieved summary flagged that the term is used without definition. The lesson gives a short working description, with legal questions going to advisers.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which guardrail does the page recommend against the 'vendor trap'?
options: Let the vendor own the repositories
Require technical standards and automated test coverage, with the client owning the repositories and CI/CD
knowledgeCheck.why: The page recommends technical standards, automated tests and client ownership of repositories and pipelines.

build.business: Cretek will add engineering capacity in more than one way. A CTO must be able to compare options on total cost and risk, and to say honestly which numbers are guesses. This is the workforce planning capability in the CTO Operating System.
build.problem: Compare hiring models for one real or realistically simulated Cretek capacity need, with a tested cost model, a sensitivity analysis, a time-zone feasibility check and a decision with guardrails.
requirements: Describe the capacity need: skills, duration, number of people, context and data sensitivity. Classify each piece of work on context, specifiability and sensitivity
Define at least four options with the three dimensions kept separate (employer, location, management model). Include at least one hybrid
Gather real quotes or market data (cited with date and currency) for rates, fees and savings, or label each input ASSUMPTION. Do not rely on the page's percentages
Compute time-zone overlap for each location pair and decide the work pattern it supports

Compute cost per effective engineer-year for each option over a one-year and a three-year horizon, including recruiting, ramp, management overhead, asynchronous loss and any vendor or employer-of-record margin
Show a sensitivity analysis over at least three of the least certain inputs, and state which inputs change the ranking
Name what the model leaves out (quality, rework, attrition, security, culture) and say how you would assess each
Write the decision rule, the guardrails (repository ownership, tests, knowledge transfer, exit terms, an exposure cap) and the review trigger as an ADR
List the legal, tax and data protection questions for qualified advisers with owners and dates. Do not state conclusions

A cost calculator that takes salary, on-cost rate, recruiting fee, rate or saving, hours, ramp months and productivity, management overhead, asynchronous loss, vendor margin and a horizon, and returns the cost per effective engineer-year; and an overlap function for two UTC offsets and working hours. Automated tests required, including the lesson's values (UTC and India overlap 2.5 hours, UTC and the Philippines no overlap, onshore permanent about 164,250 over three years), a zero horizon (reject), a negative cost (reject), a productivity loss of 100% or more (reject) and a margin of zero
A one-page summary for the CFO led by the cost range and the biggest uncertainty
Every figure labelled REAL, ASSUMPTION or SIMULATED, with currency and date
constraints: No legal or tax conclusions. Mark them as questions for advisers
Do not rank options on hourly rates alone
Do not assume ramp, savings or productivity values without labelling them
Do not give an external party sole ownership of critical-path knowledge or code without an exit plan
Must run locally with a single command for the calculator and its tests
build.design: Write a one-page design covering the need, the options, the model and its biggest uncertainty, the guardrails and one option you rejected, with the reason.
tasks: Define the options and collect inputs
Build the calculator with tests and compute costs
Write the decision record and the advisers' questions
acceptance: Options keep employer, location and management model separate
Every input is sourced or labelled as an assumption
Overlap is computed for each location pair
Cost per effective engineer-year is shown for one and three years with a sensitivity table
The model's omissions are listed with an assessment plan
Guardrails and a review trigger are recorded
Calculator tests pass including the rejection cases
No legal or tax conclusions are stated as fact
build.deliverable: The work classification, options, inputs, overlap analysis, calculator with tests, sensitivity results, decision record, advisers' questions and one-page summary, in a repository referenced by link or path.

defend.scenario: The CFO has been told offshore saves 50% to 70%. They want to know what you recommend for the migration team and how sure you are about the numbers.
prompts: Where do your savings and ramp figures come from?
Which assumption changes your ranking most?
What costs does your model leave out?
What happens to us if the vendor walks away mid-project?
How much overlap do we really have with this location?
What do we need lawyers and tax advisers to confirm?

rubric.criterion: A correct cost per effective engineer-year model with sourced or labelled inputs
Sensitivity analysis and honest identification of what drives and what is left out of the answer
A decision rule with guardrails and exit terms, with legal and tax points left to advisers
